extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on determining when a reference qualifies as a "printed publication"/prior art and how to apply 35 U.S.C. §102 (anticipation) including electronic/public-accessibility issues, date-of-availability, admissions, multiple-reference uses, inherency, and genus-species rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed Publication — Public Accessibility Test
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a "printed publication" if it is accessible to the public: "upon a satisfactory showing that such document has been disseminated or otherwise made available to the extent that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter or art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it." (In re Wyer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'printed' and 'publication' in terms of 'probability of dissemination' and 'public accessibility.' Consider evidence of dissemination or availability to persons concerned with the art. Examples and case citations (In re Wyer, I.C.E. Corp. v. Armco Steel) illustrate this unitary concept and how reproducibility/technology affects accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic Publications Count as Printed Publications if Accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication (including on-line databases or Internet publications) is a "printed publication" under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and (b) provided it was accessible to persons concerned with the art to which the document relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form (printed, handwritten, microfilm, magnetic disc, Internet pages) is immaterial; examiners should produce sufficient proof of dissemination/availability. Retain office copies when the electronic source may not be retrievable in the future. Case examples: In re Wyer, Amazon.com v. Barnesandnoble.com, In re Epstein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of Availability for Internet/Online Items
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet or on-line database disclosures are publicly available as of the date the item was publicly posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the item lacks an explicit publication/posting date (or retrieval date) and no evidence of posting date exists, it cannot be relied upon as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b). Examiners may ask the Scientific and Technical Information Center to determine earliest posting date (see MPEP §901.06(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Teachings Relied Upon from Electronic Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on an abstract only, only the abstract text (not the underlying document) may support a 102/103 rejection. When electronic and paper versions differ appreciably, cite each version separately based on what each discloses. See MPEP §§ 2121.01, 2123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of Office Copies for Electronic Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Office copies of electronic documents must be retained if the same document may not be available for retrieval in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important for Internet and online databases; retention supports reliance and reproducibility of examiner citations. See related Internet usage/citation guidance in MPEP §904.02(c) and §707.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Need to Prove Actual Examination by a Member of the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner need not prove that anyone actually looked at a publication when that publication is accessible to the public through a library or patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility and availability are the key; actual access by a member of the public is not required (e.g., In re Wyer and cases concerning library access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis in a University Library May Be Prior Art if Sufficiently Accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctoral thesis indexed and shelved in a library can be a "printed publication" if normal cataloging/indexing/shelving practices made it accessible to the public before the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence such as librarian affidavits about routine practices can establish availability. Compare cases where theses were shelved without meaningful indexing and were held not to be accessible (In re Hall; In re Cronyn; In re Bayer). The degree and meaningfulness of indexing/cataloging matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral Presentation Can Be a Printed Publication If Written Copies Are Freely Available
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper orally presented in a forum open to interested persons constitutes a "printed publication" if written copies are disseminated without restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: MIT v. AB Fortia (paper presented to 50–500 persons with written copies distributed without restriction—six persons requested copies and it was held a printed publication). An entirely oral presentation without slides/copies is not a printed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal Confidential Documents Are Not Printed Publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents distributed only internally within an organization and intended to remain confidential are not "printed publications," regardless of number of copies distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be an existing policy of confidentiality or an agreement to remain confidential; mere intent without such a policy may be insufficient. Examples: In re George; Garret Corp. v. United States; Northern Telecom v. Datapoint (restricted library access, reproduction legends, and distribution to project participants held insufficient for public accessibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Display Can Constitute a Printed Publication Even If Brief
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicly displayed document that persons of ordinary skill could see and copy can be a "printed publication" even if displayed only a few days and not disseminated or indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key inquiry: whether the reference was made 'publicly accessible.' Relevant factors (Klopfenstein): length of display, expertise of the target audience, expectations about copying, and ease/simplicity of copying. Example: poster-board slide presentation displayed at industry events for approximately three cumulative days found to be sufficiently publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of Accessibility Can Be Proven by Routine Business Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of routine business practices can establish the date on which a publication became accessible to the public; specific evidence for the exact document is not always necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Intel's usual treatment of undated specification sheets and librarian affidavits about indexing/cataloging/shelving doctoral theses (Advanced Micro-Devices; In re Hall). Such routine-practice evidence may show that undated items were publicly available before the critical date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail-Distributed Publication Effective Date Is Date Received by Public
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication disseminated by mail is not prior art until it is received by at least one member of the public; the effective date is the date when the first person receives it, not the mailing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: In re Schlittler. When relying on mailed materials, evidence of receipt by a member of the public is necessary to fix the prior-art date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by Applicant Can Constitute Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant (in the specification or during prosecution) identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission that can be relied upon in obviousness or anticipation determinations, regardless of whether the admitted work otherwise qualifies as statutory prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine whether the subject matter identified as 'prior art' is applicant's own work or another's. In absence of another credible explanation, treat such subject matter as the work of another (Riverwood; Constant). However, applicant's own earlier work is not treated as prior art unless it falls within a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion of Prior Art in Specification Treated as Admission
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification identifies work done by another as 'prior art,' that subject matter is treated as admitted prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Nomiya where figures labeled 'prior art' were treated as admission that the pictured subject matter was prior art relative to applicant's improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-Format Claims Imply Admission of Preamble Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the preamble subject matter is prior art (37 CFR 1.75(e); MPEP §608.01(m)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implied admission can be overcome if applicant gives a credible reason for Jepson format (e.g., to avoid double patenting) or where the preamble actually describes applicant's own work. Case examples: In re Fout; In re Ehrreich; Reading & Bates.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS Listing Is Not an Admission That Reference Is Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere listing of a reference in an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is not an admission that the reference is prior art against the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co.; 37 CFR 1.97(h) explicitly states that filing an IDS shall not be construed as admission that the information cited is material to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation Requires Every Claim Element to Be Taught (Expressly or Inherently)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, though identical terminology is not required (not an ipsissimis verbis test). A claim covering several alternative structures is anticipated if any one structure within the claim scope is known in the prior art. Case citations: Verdegaal Bros.; Brown v. 3M; Richardson v. Suzuki; In re Bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-Reference 35 U.S.C. 102 Rejections Limited to Specific Purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally only one reference should be used in a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection, but multiple references may be proper to (A) prove the primary reference contains an enabled disclosure, (B) explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference, or (C) show that a characteristic not disclosed is inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using extra references, the examiner must fit the use into one of these permitted categories and provide appropriate evidence and reasoning. See MPEP §2131.01 and paragraphs I–III for examples and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Extra References to Show the Primary Reference Is Enabled
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional reference may be relied upon to show that the primary reference provides an "enabled disclosure" (i.e., that the public had sufficient information to make/use the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Samour; In re Donohue—when a publication disclosed the claimed structure and other patents showed methods of making the class, the publications taught all elements and patents supported enablement/documentation of public possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Extrinsic Evidence to Explain a Term's Meaning in the Primary Reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain (but not to expand) the meaning of terms and phrases used in the primary reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Baxter Travenol Labs.—depositions, declarations, and admissions established that 'commercial blood bags' meant bags containing DEHP, so the reference was read as disclosing the additive. Extrinsic evidence must explain the meaning as understood by those of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Extra Evidence to Show an Inherent Characteristic of the Primary Reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence can be used to show that a characteristic not expressly disclosed in the primary reference is nonetheless inherent in what the reference describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Controlling cases: Continental Can Co. v. Monsanto; Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO; In re King; Titanium Metals v. Banner. Evidence of inherency can include test data and expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-Species Rule — A Species Anticipates a Genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic claim cannot be allowed if the prior art discloses a species falling within the claimed genus; the species will anticipate the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Slayter; In re Gosteli. If a prior art reference discloses at least one claimed species, the genus claim is anticipated unless applicant has an earlier priority date that avoids the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference That Clearly Names Claimed Species Anticipates the Species
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference clearly names the claimed species, that reference anticipates the species claim regardless of how many other species are named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte A (Merck Index analogy)—a specific compound listed among many is still 'described' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. §102(a). In re Sivaramakrishnan offers similar principle for additives named among many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Chemical Formula Anticipates a Species Only If the Species Can Be 'At Once Envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art discloses a generic chemical formula with lists of substituents, anticipation of a specific compound requires that the specific species be "at once envisaged" from the formula (i.e., one of ordinary skill can immediately draw the structure or write the name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to whether classes of substituents are sufficiently limited/well-delineated; preferred embodiments can show limitation. Cases: Ex parte A; In re Petering; In re Schauman. If the generic formula encompasses a vast/infinite number of compounds, it generally does not anticipate a specific compound unless the formula+preferred lists narrow the possibilities to the point that the specific compound is readily envisaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Laid-Open Patent Applications — Confirm Date of Publication Before Relying
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of a foreign patent application should not be relied upon as prior art until the date of publication (i.e., insertion into the laid-open application) can be confirmed by an examiner’s review of a copy of the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §901.05; In re Wyer example where laid-open Australian application (with microfilming and diazo copies) was held to be a 'printed publication' after factual review of accessibility and distribution; always confirm publication date and availability evidence before treating foreign applications as prior art.
